stages.name: Money supply and inflation
stages.title: Money supply and inflation
stages.sub: After this, the student can explain why economists link a growing money supply to inflation.

steps.q: Notes, coins and money held in bank accounts across the whole economy are added up. What is being measured?
steps.right: The total amount of money in the economy
steps.wrong: The total value of goods sold in the economy
steps.hint: Think about cash plus bank deposits, not what gets bought with them.

steps.q: The government wants one figure for how much money exists in the economy this year. What kind of figure does it need?
steps.right: A measure of the total stock of money
steps.wrong: A measure of how fast prices are rising
steps.hint: You already worked out what the total amount of money is called. What would tracking that total be called?

steps.q: A £10 note buys coffee, then bread, then flour as it changes hands. Has it supported more than £10 of spending?
steps.right: Yes, because it changed hands several times
steps.wrong: No, it can only ever support £10 of spending
steps.hint: Count how many purchases that one note was involved in, not just its face value.

steps.q: A country's prices double in a year, but it produces exactly the same goods and services. Has it really produced more?
steps.right: No, only the money value has risen
steps.wrong: Yes, it has produced twice as much
steps.hint: Doubled prices with unchanged goods: is anything more actually being made?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Money supply times how often it circulates always equals price level times real output. What kind of relationship is that?
steps.right: An equation that must always balance
steps.wrong: A rough estimate that often fails to hold
steps.hint: Every pound spent by a buyer is a pound received by a seller, in every single transaction.

steps.q: If velocity and real output barely change in the short run and the money supply doubles, what must happen to the price level?
steps.wrong: It stays the same, since output is unchanged
steps.hint: If two sides of an equation must stay equal, and one side doubles while V and Q on the other side stay fixed, what has to move?

steps.q: If velocity and output are roughly fixed and money supply keeps growing faster than output, what happens to prices over time?
